item.title: How to leave WordPress without losing anything
item.description:
The short answer

Leaving WordPress is not moving files: it is keeping addresses, content and links while you change the machinery that publishes them. If the addresses are kept, rankings are kept. If they change without redirects, they are lost.

Why people leave

It is rarely ideology. It is usually one of three things:

  • Maintenance: weekly updates, plugins that break, nobody watching.
  • Speed: the site is slow because there is more machinery than needed.
  • Fear: fear that an update breaks the site, fear of attacks, fear of touching anything.

What is kept and what is lost

Kept: addresses (with parity and redirects), texts, images, files, publication dates and authorship where present.

item.title: Hugo or WordPress: which one fits you
item.description:
The short answer

Hugo if the site publishes information and you want few parts that can break. WordPress if you need a shop, users, a complex editorial workflow or an ecosystem of extensions that already covers your case.

The comparison, in one table

Criterion Hugo (static site) WordPress
Maintenance Almost none: no database Constant: core, plugins and backups
Speed Very high: pre-built files Depends on hosting and plugins
Attack surface Small: no admin panel Large: the most attacked target on the web
Editing Visual editor on text files Panel with menus and roles
Shop and users No (needs external services) Yes, built in
Extensions Few, and often not needed Thousands, with their maintenance
Bulk publishing Very good Very good
People who can work on it Fewer, but you never need to Many, and often you do

When Hugo fits you

  • Sites from 5 to 200 pages that inform about something: a cultural space, a band, a studio, a publisher, a restaurant.
  • Projects where nobody wants to think about updates.
  • Sites that must load fast on mobile and work in difficult conditions.
  • Projects where visitors’ data must not pass through third parties.

When WordPress fits you

  • A shop with stock, variants, coupons and shipping (WooCommerce).
  • A member area or courses with registrations and student tracking.
  • An editorial workflow with many roles, calendars and approvals.
  • When your team is already trained in WordPress and you just want to maintain it well.
  • When you depend on a very specific plugin that does exactly what you need.

What an agency selling WordPress will not tell you

That the real cost is not building the site: it is maintaining it. A site with fifteen plugins is monthly work someone must do — or nobody does. Many security and speed problems we see are not WordPress, they are that work not being paid for.

item.title: Your WordPress is slow or got attacked: how to find out why
item.description:
The short answer

A slow or attacked WordPress almost never has a single cause. It is diagnosed by measuring three things: what the server sends, what the browser loads and what the admin area does. Without that data, “optimising” means changing things at random.

The usual causes, by frequency

  1. Overloaded shared hosting. The site is not slow: the neighbour is eating the machine.
  2. Plugins. Many, badly built or abandoned. Often there are fifteen and three are used.
  3. Bloated database. Revisions, transients, trash and old analytics tables.
  4. Unoptimised images. A 4 MB hero makes the site feel slow even when the server is fine.
  5. Automated attacks. Password guessing and mass requests to the admin area.
  6. Heavy theme. Page builders that load half a megabyte of code to show a headline.

How to diagnose it (without guessing)

  • Measure the server response time on a simple page.
  • Measure the weight and number of files on the homepage.
  • Check access logs: repeated attempts at wp-login or xmlrpc.
  • Check disk space and database health.
  • Review which plugins are active and which have never been updated.
  • Check certificate, backups and PHP version.

What to do depending on the result

  • Overloaded server → change hosting or hosting model.
  • Plugins → remove them, do not just deactivate.
  • Database → clean and limit revisions.
  • Images → convert and serve proper sizes.
  • Attacks → firewall, access limits and, if needed, take the admin panel off the internet.
  • All at once → maybe the question is not how to fix it, but whether this site should be a WordPress at all.

When the fix is not migrating

If the site sells, manages members or has a complex editorial workflow, changing technology fixes nothing: what exists needs care. Migrating is a solution for sites that only publish and demand more maintenance than they give back.

item.title: Moving from Blogger to your own site
item.description:
The short answer

Leaving Blogger is mostly about taking the content out of Google’s cloud: posts, images and comments. Addresses are kept, but images must be downloaded and hosted on your own infrastructure, because today they live on Google servers.

Why people leave

  • Control: content sits on a platform that decides for you (design, templates, features).
  • Speed and looks: Blogger templates are far behind what can be done today.
  • Trust: platforms that shut services or change terms. It has happened before.
  • Sovereignty: photos, texts and comments are yours, but you do not hold them.

What to preserve

  • The posts, with date, author and tags.
  • The images, which today point at Google servers.
  • The addresses of each post and each tag.
  • The comments, if you want to keep them.
  • The domain, which is what makes nothing change place.

The 9 Barris Imatge case

A photography collective in Nou Barris has documented the neighbourhood since 2002, and since 2008 published it on Blogger. 3,006 posts written by people who do photography, not IT.

item.title: What a band's website needs to cover
item.description:
The short answer

A band’s website is not a shop window: it is the place where someone who does not know you decides whether to listen to you, book you or move on. They do it in a few seconds with four questions: who you are, what you sound like, when you play and how to book you. If the site answers them without making people think, the rest is decoration.
